extracted.intended_audience: digital humanists, meme practitioners, and scholars studying Internet culture
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly review of Limor Shifman's Memes in Digital Culture that summarizes definitions, differentiations, success factors, and research opportunities for studying Internet memes. Aimed at guiding academics and practitioners on conceptualizing and researching digital memes and virality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dawkins's meme transmission properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For memes to spread successfully they must possess three properties: 'longevity, fecundity, and copying-fidelity' (Dawkins).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifman applies these properties to online memes: online transmission increases copy fidelity (lossless digitization), greatly increases fecundity (many copies in a short time), and may increase longevity via indefinite archival storage. The review notes tension between Dawkins's emphasis on exact copying and later arguments about remixing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifman's definition of Internet memes
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet memes are defined as: '(a) a group of digital items sharing common characteristics of content, form, and/or stance, which (b) were created with awareness of each other, and (c) were circulated, imitated, and/or transformed via the Internet by many users' (Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition purposely treats memes as groups of related items (not single viral items), and includes imitation, transformation, and circulation as core behaviors. It also emphasizes shared characteristics (content/form/stance) and creator/user awareness of the relationship among items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to resolve three foundational issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Before memes can be integrated meaningfully into academia and industry, three issues must be resolved: agreeing on an exact definition of 'meme'; differentiating 'meme' from 'viral'; and conducting more studies that examine the practices and politics behind memes (Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three issues are framed as the platform for subsequent research and practice; the review uses them to organize critique and research recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre taxonomy of Internet memes
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifman categorizes nine specific meme genres into three general groups: documentation of real-life moments, explicit manipulation of content, and creation of a 'new universe' of meme-oriented content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the review doesn't list all nine genres in detail, it notes the taxonomy's usefulness for practitioners and scholars in categorizing subject matter and guiding analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and framing of 'viral' content
rubrics_metrics.description: A viral is 'a single cultural unit (formulated in words, image or video) that is spread by multiple agents and is viewed by many millions' (Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifman advises thinking of memes and virals as two ends of a dynamic spectrum rather than wholly separate categories; a meme can start as a viral. Virality research generally aligns with the transmission model (marketing/politics), while memetics aligns with the ritual model (cultural participation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Ps of virality
rubrics_metrics.description: Six factors that explain content virality: positivity (and humor), provocation (high emotions), packaging (content organization), prestige (of the author), positioning (page placement), and participation (audience involvement) (from Berger & Milkman study, highlighted by Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors arose from a large study of New York Times articles; they are recommended as levers to influence virality when designing or studying content. Positivity/humor and participation overlap with memetic features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features characteristic of memetic videos
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic videos tend to include ordinary people, flawed masculinity, humor, and repetitiveness (actors repeating something over and over) (Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These recurring features help explain why certain videos invite remixing and imitation; repetitiveness is highlighted as a memetic potential that facilitates derivative creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features characteristic of memetic photos
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic photos often include a juxtaposition between the actor and surrounding elements (deepened ridicule of the original) or people in frozen-motion poses that create a ludicrous posture (Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juxtaposition can present a puzzle or problem that viewers solve by remixing/contextualizing; frozen-motion poses create visual comedy conducive to replication and variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared features of memes and virals
rubrics_metrics.description: Both memes and virals commonly include simple packaging, humor, and tools to engage viewer participation (Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These commonalities explain overlap between the phenomena and why some items function as both; designers/researchers should consider these elements when analyzing spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features unique to virality
rubrics_metrics.description: Features unique to virality include prestige of the author, positioning (e.g., page placement), and emotional content (Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because virality often relies on transmission by influential nodes and high-arousal emotion, marketing/political actors can leverage prestige and placement to boost spread; these are less central to memetic remix cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features unique to memetic success
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic-unique features include memetic potential (e.g., repetition) and the presence of a puzzle or problem that requires solving (such as figuring out a juxtaposition) (Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties encourage user engagement through remixing and reinterpretation, fostering derivative works rather than mere forwarding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and social functions of memes
rubrics_metrics.description: Political Internet memes serve three interwoven functions: to persuade or advocate for political candidates; to empower grassroots activities by citizens; and to provide an inexpensive, accessible, and enjoyable mode of public expression (Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memes can constitute political participation and democratic subversion (e.g., localized manipulation in censored contexts). Researchers should treat memes as meaningful political actors, not mere entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-generated globalization and localization
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes 'are rarely confined to a single geographic location' and often undergo 'user-generated globalization' where ordinary users localize, translate, and distribute memes globally (Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phenomenon contrasts with corporate localization; scholars should study how grassroots translation/localization influences meme meaning and lifecycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological guidance for digital humanists
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital humanists can create provocative/promotional illustrations or derive memes to post on platforms (Tumblr, Memes.com, Reddit) and then monitor views, comments, and derivative postings; applying the 'six Ps' can help influence memetic interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review suggests practical classroom and research projects: have students create memes and track lifecycles to teach rhetorical strategies and study propagation, modification, and cross-cultural interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promising research areas in memetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Four promising areas for research: politics of memetic participation; Internet memes as a language; memes and political change; and viral and memetic success (Shifman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These topics are presented as gaps in the literature and as invitations for further scholarship; the review emphasizes that more empirical studies and theoretical refinement are needed.
